title: Stdlib - String vs char*
description:
## Two ways to store text in C++

### char* (C-style string)
A raw pointer to an array of characters ending with `\0` (null terminator).
```cpp
const char* name = "CBitOS";
// In memory: ['C','B','i','t','O','S','\0']
```
- No `.length()`, no `.append()`, no safety
- Use `strlen()`, `strcmp()`, `strcpy()` from `<cstring>`
- Easy to cause buffer overflows and memory bugs

### std::string (C++ string)
A class that manages memory for you.
```cpp
std::string name = "CBitOS";
name.append(" v2");  // just works
```
- Has `.length()`, `.substr()`, `.find()`, etc.
- Grows automatically
- Safe

### Converting between them:
```cpp
std::string s = "hello";
const char* c = s.c_str();  // string -> char*
std::string s2 = std::string(c);  // char* -> string
```


---
## Assignment:
CBitOS has a legacy function that takes `const char*`. Given the `std::string version`, convert it to a `const char*` and print it. Then create a `const char*` kernel name and convert it to `std::string` and print its length.
